tagline: A riverbank road through a village shaped by ocean-going shipbuilding
intro: Middle Haddam Road follows the Connecticut River’s east bank through a village constrained by steep slopes and stream valleys. The last 1.51 miles of Route 151 have state scenic-road designation, ending at Route 66 in Cobalt. Along this short stretch, Middle Haddam’s historic district contains 58 significant primary buildings, most built before 1835. Their predominantly Federal character belongs to the village’s years as a river port.

By the American Revolution, Middle Haddam was a commercial center for farmland to the east and a focus of the roads serving it. The village handled shipments to the West Indies and North American coast, and its yards built ocean-going vessels. The later Moodus–Haddam Neck–Cobalt highway became state Highway 167 in the 1920s. Renumbering in 1932 incorporated it into Route 151.

Approaching from the south, Route 151 passes the Hurd State Park access road before reaching Middle Haddam. Continue north through the village toward Cobalt, where the older port district gives way to later industrial development and the road meets Route 66.

moments.title: Hurd State Park
moments.text: Hurd State Park lies on the east bank of the Connecticut River, south of Middle Haddam. The state bought its first 150 acres in 1914, then faced a dispute over mining rights when Jesse S. Miller claimed the property’s feldspar. The state prevailed in the Connecticut State Supreme Court in 1935. The park now offers hiking, picnicking and mountain biking, as well as primitive camping for boaters on the river.

moments.title: Dart Island State Park
moments.text: Dart Island is a wooded sandbar in the Connecticut River, reachable only by boat. Fishermen once used it for the hickory shad runs, building a shed and equipment to manage their fishing lines. Russell Dart donated the approximately 1.5-acre island to the state in 1918. Its reported size then varied: official publications rounded it to two acres, while an unofficial 1924 claim called it the country’s smallest state park at one acre. The state’s 2012 Register and Manual listed 19 acres. Willow, poplar and red maple grow on the undeveloped island, which has no public facilities.

moments.title: Middle Haddam
moments.text: Shipbuilding gave Middle Haddam connections beyond the Connecticut River. A sawmill operated on Mill Brook, a ferry crossed the river by the early 18th century, and the village became a shipping point for trade with the West Indies and the North American coast. Its shipyards built vessels for ocean voyages. The village’s shape reflects the terrain: river to the west, steep banks and stream valleys inland. Most of the historic district’s 58 significant primary buildings predate 1835, and the oldest date to 1732. Among this predominantly Federal architecture, a single Queen Anne Victorian summer residence stands near the town landing.
